subChunks.title: When Science Fails to Replicate: Causes, Consequences, and Responses
subChunks.hookHtml: In 2011, Daryl Bem published a paper in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology — one of psychology's most prestigious outlets — reporting that participants could feel the future. His 'precognition' experiments found statistically significant evidence that people's physiological responses anticipated randomly selected erotic images before those images were shown. The paper passed peer review. It was methodologically orthodox by the standards of the day. And it was almost certainly wrong. What Bem's paper did was make visible a problem that had been growing silently for decades: the standard practices of psychological research — small samples, flexible analysis choices, selective reporting — were generating a literature full of findings that could not withstand independent scrutiny. Over the next five years, a coordinated effort to replicate 100 psychology studies found that only 36–39% reproduced the original effect at a comparable magnitude. The replication crisis was not a scandal caused by a few dishonest researchers. It was a systemic failure — and understanding it is the most important intellectual challenge facing psychology in the twenty-first century.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Scale of the Problem

The Reproducibility Project: Psychology (Open Science Collaboration, 2015) attempted to replicate 100 published psychology studies using the original methods. The results were stark: only 36% produced a statistically significant result in the same direction; effect sizes in replications were on average half the size of original studies; studies in cognitive psychology replicated at higher rates than social psychology studies. A subsequent meta-scientific study of 21 high-profile social science findings (Camerer et al., 2018) found 13 of 21 replicated, but with average effect sizes 50% smaller than originals. The replication problem is not unique to psychology — medicine, economics, and biology all face similar crises — but psychology's effect has been particularly publicly damaging, especially for findings that had entered popular culture: power posing (Cuddy), ego depletion (Baumeister), social priming (Bargh), and many others.

Causes: Questionable Research Practices

Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn (2011) introduced the concept of the researcher degrees of freedom — the many flexible decisions researchers make during data collection and analysis that, when exploited, dramatically inflate false-positive rates. They demonstrated through simulation that with common flexibility — choosing which of several dependent variables to report, deciding when to stop collecting data, including or excluding covariates — the false-positive rate for a 'significant' finding at p < .05 could reach 60% rather than the nominal 5%.

p-hacking describes the practice (often unconscious) of continuing to analyse data, add participants, or try different analyses until a significant p-value appears. HARKing (Hypothesising After Results are Known — Kerr, 1998) describes presenting post-hoc hypotheses as if they were a priori predictions, inflating the apparent confirmatory power of the findings. Together with publication bias — journals' preference for significant results meaning null results remain in file drawers — these practices produce a scientific literature systematically biased toward false-positive findings that are larger than the true effect.

Simonsohn, Nelson, and Simmons (2014) developed p-curve analysis to detect evidential value in sets of significant results: if a set of studies has genuine power to detect a real effect, the distribution of p-values should be right-skewed (many small p-values); if the literature is p-hacked, p-values will cluster just below .05. P-curve analysis of several prominent literatures showed evidence of widespread p-hacking.

Structural Causes

Beyond individual researcher behaviour, the replication crisis reflects structural incentives in academic science. Publication in high-impact journals requires novel, significant findings. Grants require preliminary data showing significant effects. Academic careers depend on publication counts in prestigious outlets. This incentive structure rewards positive, surprising findings and punishes null results, careful replication attempts, and transparent reporting of failures. The result is a publication system that efficiently filters out disconfirmatory evidence — the exact opposite of what Popperian science requires.

Importantly, most researchers engaging in questionable research practices are not deliberately deceiving: they believe their hypotheses are true, interpret ambiguous analytical choices in ways that align with expectations, and genuinely do not recognise the cumulative inflation this produces. The crisis is systemic, not primarily about individual dishonesty (though outright fraud — Stapel, Sanna, Förster — also occurred and went undetected for years).

The Open Science Response

The replication crisis has generated a substantial reform movement — open science — aimed at changing both practices and incentives:

Pre-registration: Researchers register hypotheses, design, sample size, and analysis plan before data collection, time-stamped on repositories like OSF (Open Science Framework) or AsPredicted. This separates confirmatory from exploratory analyses and prevents HARKing. Pre-registration does not prevent exploratory analyses — it distinguishes them from confirmatory tests.

Registered Reports: A publication format in which peer review occurs before data collection — the journal evaluates the introduction and methods and, if the design is sound, commits to publishing the findings regardless of outcome. This removes publication bias at source and is now offered by over 300 journals.

Open data and open materials: Sharing raw data and analysis code on repositories (OSF, GitHub) enables independent verification, error correction, and reanalysis. The Psychological Science Accelerator demonstrates the power of large-scale collaborative data collection across many labs and cultures simultaneously.

Statistical reform: Growing advocacy for effect size reporting and confidence intervals over binary significance testing; Bayesian methods that quantify evidence for and against hypotheses; equivalence testing to establish when effects are negligibly small; and calls to abandon the .05 threshold altogether (Benjamin et al., 2018 proposed raising it to .005 for claiming 'significance').

Critical Perspectives on Open Science

The open science movement is not without its own critics. Some argue that pre-registration is too rigid for exploratory research and may stifle discovery. Others note that open data can enable 'data dredging' by others even when the original researcher was disciplined. Questions arise about whose research gets pre-registered and in which languages — whether open science inadvertently advantages well-resourced Western institutions. And there is a deeper methodological question: whether the replication crisis reflects fundamental problems with NHST-based quantitative psychology, or whether it is a correctable problem of practice. The crisis has also been used, sometimes unfairly, to dismiss entire bodies of research: the fact that some social psychology studies fail to replicate does not mean social psychology as a discipline produces no reliable knowledge.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen projects a single image: a funnel plot of 100 psychology replications, the original effects clustered near the top, the replications scattered and shrunken below. She says nothing for a moment.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: This is the most important graph in contemporary psychology. Not because it shows psychology is broken — it isn't — but because it shows what happens when you build an incentive structure that rewards novelty and significance above everything else. We created a literature that was scientifically unreliable, not because researchers were dishonest, but because the system selected for false positives as efficiently as natural selection selects for adaptation.

A student protests: 'But if 36% replicated, isn't that actually quite low?' Dr. Chen nods. 'It depends on your prior expectations. If you thought every published finding in social psychology was probably true, 36% is catastrophic. If you thought many findings were probably noise, it's confirmatory. The real lesson is that we should have had better tools to distinguish from the start.'

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: The good news is that psychology is doing something medicine, economics, and other fields haven't managed nearly as well: confronting the problem openly, studying itself scientifically, and changing. Pre-registration, registered reports, open data — these aren't just methodological reforms. They're a change in the epistemic culture of the field. And that's genuinely exciting.

She pauses at a quote projected behind her — Feynman: 'The first principle is that you must not fool yourself — and you are the easiest person to fool.' 'Open science,' she says, 'is institutional infrastructure for Feynman's first principle.'

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why a study being published in a prestigious scientific journal does not guarantee its findings are true — and what the open science movement is doing about it.
learningObjectives: Describe the scale and scope of the replication crisis in psychology, citing the OSC (2015) Reproducibility Project findings
Explain the key questionable research practices (p-hacking, HARKing, publication bias) and how they inflate false-positive rates
Evaluate the main open science reforms (pre-registration, registered reports, open data) and their limitations
Critically assess arguments for and against the view that the replication crisis represents a fundamental failure of psychological science
commonMistakes: Concluding that the replication crisis means all of psychology is wrong — many robust findings do replicate, particularly in cognitive psychology and psychophysics
Treating p-hacking as deliberate fraud — most questionable research practices are unconscious and reflect systemic incentive problems rather than individual dishonesty
Conflating pre-registration with rigidity — pre-registered studies can still conduct exploratory analyses; pre-registration distinguishes these from confirmatory tests
Ignoring the cross-disciplinary nature of the problem — medicine, economics, and biology face parallel crises, suggesting structural causes rather than psychology-specific failings
assessmentCriteria: Demonstrates sophisticated understanding of how incentive structures (not just individual behaviour) drive questionable research practices
Evaluates open science reforms with appropriate nuance — acknowledging benefits and limitations rather than treating them as panaceas
Engages critically with debates about whether quantitative reform is sufficient or whether deeper methodological pluralism is needed
Shows awareness of equity and access dimensions of open science — who benefits, whose research gets pre-registered, and what is missing from the reform agenda
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: A psychology researcher tells you: 'I ran my study and the results were just below significance (p = .07). I collected twenty more participants and now p = .03. It was significant all along — I just didn't have enough power initially.' Identify the questionable research practice being described, explain why it inflates false-positive rates, and describe how pre-registration would prevent this problem.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Questionable research practice: The researcher is engaged in optional stopping (a form of p-hacking) — continuing to collect data until a significant result is obtained, then stopping. This is a researcher degree of freedom that violates the assumptions of frequentist null hypothesis significance testing. NHST assumes that the sample size is fixed before data collection; if the researcher peeks at results and continues collecting only when the test is non-significant, the Type I error rate inflates dramatically beyond the nominal .05. Simmons et al. (2011) showed that with optional stopping (collecting up to n = 50 in batches of 10), the false-positive rate can reach 22% for a 5% nominal α.

Why it inflates false positives: The p-value under NHST is only interpretable if the stopping rule is pre-specified. When researchers stop based on the observed p-value, they exploit the random fluctuations in p over the course of data collection. At any given point, there is a reasonable probability of crossing the significance threshold by chance; continuing to sample until this happens means the 'significant' finding may be pure noise.

How pre-registration prevents this: If the researcher had pre-registered their study on OSF or AsPredicted before collecting data, they would have specified their target sample size based on an a priori power analysis. This commitment is time-stamped and publicly visible. Collecting additional participants after seeing a p = .07 result would represent a deviation from the pre-registered protocol, which reviewers and readers could identify. Pre-registration does not make optional stopping impossible — a researcher could still violate their plan — but it creates accountability and makes post-hoc deviations transparent rather than invisible.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: The registered reports publication format has been described as 'the most important methodological innovation in psychology in decades' (Munafo et al., 2017). Write a critical evaluation (600–800 words) of registered reports as a solution to the replication crisis. Your answer should: (a) explain how registered reports work and why they address publication bias; (b) identify at least two genuine limitations or criticisms of the format; and (c) assess whether registered reports alone are sufficient to restore confidence in psychological science, or whether broader systemic changes are also needed.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
How registered reports work and why they address publication bias: In a registered report, peer review is split into two stages. Stage 1 occurs before data collection: the journal evaluates the theoretical rationale, hypotheses, methods, and analysis plan. If the design is judged sound, the journal issues an in-principle acceptance (IPA) — a commitment to publish the findings regardless of whether they are significant or not. Stage 2 occurs after data collection: reviewers assess whether the authors adhered to the registered protocol and whether conclusions follow from results. The format addresses publication bias at source because the publication decision is made before outcomes are known. Journals cannot preferentially accept significant findings if they commit to publishing before seeing them. This removes the core structural incentive for p-hacking, HARKing, and selective reporting.

Genuine limitations: First, registered reports are poorly suited to exploratory and discovery-oriented research. Science advances not only through confirmatory hypothesis-testing but through unexpected observations, serendipitous findings, and creative data exploration. A culture that over-valorises pre-registration may inhibit the kind of flexible, theory-building inquiry that generates the hypotheses that later get rigorously tested. Second, registered reports do not eliminate all questionable practices: researchers can still deviate from their pre-registered plan in Stage 2, sometimes with post-hoc justifications that are difficult for reviewers to evaluate. Protocol deviations may be subtle — small changes in exclusion criteria, covariate adjustment, or outcome operationalisation — and reviewers rarely have the power to detect them without full data access. Third, registered reports are more time-consuming and require a level of methodological planning that disadvantages researchers in resource-poor settings, early-career researchers without senior mentorship, and researchers working in areas where power analyses are difficult to specify in advance (e.g., qualitative-adjacent quantitative work, novel paradigms).

Whether registered reports alone are sufficient: Registered reports are a powerful but partial solution. They address the specific problem of publication bias in confirmatory research, but they do not address: (a) the systemic incentive structures that reward novelty over replication — registered reports of null results are publishable in principle, but are they actually prioritised by editors?; (b) the accumulation of the pre-crisis literature — the thousands of unreplicated findings already in textbooks and informing policy; (c) the cultural dimensions of reproducibility — how psychology is taught, how scientists are trained, and what counts as a career-defining finding. A complete reform agenda requires changes in journal incentives, grant agency priorities (funding for replication and null-result studies), training curricula (statistics education, open science norms), institutional incentives (hiring and promotion criteria emphasising rigour over impact factor), and collective norm shifts about what constitutes admirable science. Registered reports are one crucial tool in this broader project, not a standalone solution.

questions.questionHtml: The Open Science Collaboration (2015) Reproducibility Project attempted to replicate 100 psychology studies. Approximately what percentage produced a statistically significant result in the same direction as the original?
questions.explanationHtml: The OSC (2015) found that approximately 36–39% of replications produced a significant result in the same direction. Effect sizes in replications were on average half those of original studies, indicating systematic inflation in the original literature.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher analyses their dataset five different ways and reports only the analysis that yields p = .04. This is best described as:
options: p-hacking via researcher degrees of freedom
questions.correctAnswer: p-hacking via researcher degrees of freedom
questions.explanationHtml: Trying multiple analyses and reporting only the significant one is a classic example of exploiting researcher degrees of freedom — a form of p-hacking. HARKing refers specifically to presenting hypotheses as a priori when they were generated post-hoc. Publication bias refers to journals' preference for significant results. Both p-hacking and HARKing are individual researcher-level practices, distinct from publication bias which is a journal/editorial-level phenomenon.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following is the strongest argument that the replication crisis does NOT represent a fundamental failure of psychological science?
options: Most published psychological studies use appropriate statistical methods
Cognitive psychology studies replicate at substantially higher rates than social psychology, suggesting the problem is specific to certain paradigms rather than the entire field
Bem's precognition study was eventually retracted
Open science reforms have now been widely adopted by major journals
questions.correctAnswer: Cognitive psychology studies replicate at substantially higher rates than social psychology, suggesting the problem is specific to certain paradigms rather than the entire field
questions.explanationHtml: The differential replication rates across sub-fields (cognitive psychology replicating better than social psychology) suggests the crisis is not uniformly distributed — some domains produce more reliable knowledge than others. This supports a targeted rather than wholesale dismissal. The other options are less compelling: statistical methods were broadly appropriate; Bem's paper was not formally retracted; and open science adoption, while growing, is incomplete and does not validate the pre-crisis literature.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A meta-analytic tool assessing whether a set of significant results contains a true effect; genuine effects produce right-skewed p-value distributions; p-hacked literatures cluster just below .05.
A statistical index expressing the relative evidence for one hypothesis over another; unlike p-values, Bayesian factors can quantify evidence for the null hypothesis.
A statistical approach testing whether an effect is smaller than a specified minimum meaningful size, enabling formal inference about the absence of a practically significant effect.
A publication format where peer review and in-principle acceptance occur before data collection, removing publication bias; over 300 journals now offer this format.
A free open-source platform (osf.io) for registering studies, pre-registering hypotheses, sharing data and materials, and collaborating on research.
The Granularity-Related Inconsistency of Means test — a mathematical check for whether a reported mean is consistent with the sample size and scale granularity.
A method examining how a statistical result changes across all reasonable analytical decisions, producing a curve of estimates rather than a single point.
A systematic approach examining how results vary across multiple plausible analytical specifications, providing transparent picture of analytical sensitivity.
